comments.capsule: Where the law seems to legislate about oxen, what was written for human beings contains a teaching about the nature of things.
comments.comment: … For he would have seen that “God does not care for oxen” (1 Corinthians 9:9), even where He seems to be making laws about oxen or animals without reason (Deuteronomy 25:4), but that what was written for the sake of human beings (1 Corinthians 9:10), under the outward appearance of dealing with animals without reason, contains a teaching about the nature of things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the law about oxen is read as written for human beings.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Everywhere the law legislates for equality and exact justice, as in the command for a true weight and measure.
comments.comment: … For everywhere the law is seen legislating, providing for equality, and making the exact test of the just. For it has been written in Deuteronomy: ‘There will not be in your bag a great or small weight; a true just weight will be for you, and a true just measure will be for you, in order that you may become many-dayed upon the earth which the Lord your God gives you in a lot, because an abomination to the Lord your God is everyone doing these things, everyone doing an unjust thing.’ (Deuteronomy 25:13-16) …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: The wife is the old covenant, which the nations have gained; the house is the fallen temple; the vineyard bore thorns.
comments.comment: … “You shall take a wife”: the old covenant; “and another man shall have her”: for the people from the nations has gained it. “You shall build a house, and you shall not live in it”: the temple, plainly, for you see it fallen. “You shall plant a vineyard, and you shall not gather its grapes”: for it bore not grapes but thorns (Isaiah 5:2). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains each threat of the verse and how it came about.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: Christ the vine came from them but we gather his grapes, and his sacrifice was theirs but the supper is ours.
comments.comment: [The vineyard can also mean Christ,] for Christ came from them (Romans 9:5), the vine of our life (John 15:1); but it is we who gather his grapes, we who mix the wine, we who drink the new wine. “Your calf shall be slaughtered before you, and you shall not eat of it”: for theirs is the sacrifice of Christ – they led the calf from heaven up to the altar – but ours is the supper, ours the table.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the vineyard not gathered and the calf not eaten as fulfilled in Christ.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: The proselyte rising above Israel describes a change of circumstances, as Gentiles who believe now stand above those who turn from the gospel.
comments.comment: Concerning these proselytes, Moses said to Israel, saying, 'If you do not obey the commandments of the Lord your God, the proselyte who is among you will be above you, but you will be below' (Deuteronomy 28:43), through the changing of circumstances. Indeed, before the coming of the Savior, those of the Gentiles who hurried to worship God approached Israel being instructed and obeying them; but now, those who wish to approach the faith of Christ from the Israelites are setting aside the evangelical commonwealth, approaching as sacrifices among those of the Gentiles who have believed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the saying about the proselyte rising above Israel was fulfilled.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who once came to the law as proselytes now lead the assembly that draws near to God, and the synagogues follow.
comments.comment: … the synagogues of the Jews would most fittingly be second and following, according to 'The first will be last and the last first' (Matthew 20:16), and 'The proselyte among you will rise above you as head, and you will be as the tail' (Deuteronomy 28:43-44). For those who long ago became proselytes of the law in order to be made close to God now themselves lead the assembly that draws near to God, …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The life that hangs before their eyes is Christ on the wood of the cross, and their unbelief has become the cause of fear.
comments.comment: … they fell sick with unbelief, brought ignorance instead of knowledge, and at the time for theology slid into blasphemy. They entered the bridal chamber and did not receive the Bridegroom; they wreathed the wedding hall and refused the marriage; and when the cross was carried out, the elements were shaken, but they were not changed. For this is what he added next: “And your life shall hang before your eyes” (Deuteronomy 28:66). What is the life? Christ, who says: “I am the way and the life and the truth” (John 14:6). And where does it hang? On the wood of the cross. For he who hung the earth by a word (Job 26:7) hangs on the wood; on it he who carries is carried, he who suspends is suspended, he who lifts up is lifted up: “For when I am lifted up,” he says, “I will draw all to myself” (John 12:32). “And you shall fear day and night, and you shall not believe in your life” (Deuteronomy 28:66). So unbelief has become the cause of fear.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'your life shall hang before your eyes' meant.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: The prophecy was fulfilled in those who did not believe the Life among men.
comments.comment: … And in you the prophecy is fulfilled that says, “Your life will be hanging before your eyes, and you will not believe your life” (Deuteronomy 28:66). For you did not believe the Life that had come to dwell among the human race.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The signs at the cross, the earthquake and the darkened sun, made them afraid, so that they asked when evening would come.
comments.comment: … Because of the signs and wonders that were being done at the time of the cross – the earth quaking, the sun fleeing, the sky hiding, the rocks splitting, the veil tearing, the tombs opening (Matthew 27:51-52) – they were afraid and troubled, and so they were naturally driven to say to one another: “When will it be evening, so that we may take the Life down from the cross, hide in the earth the one who came from heaven, …
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: Love attentive to God is luminous and so prepares long, many-dayed life for those who share in it.
comments.comment: … the prophet of the divine laws, Moses, [is] saying to the God-lover: 'This is your life and the length of your days: to love the Lord your God with all your soul and with all your heart' (Deut 6:5). For since love that is attentive to God is luminous, it prepares long and great days, so that those participating in it find themselves having many-dayed and long-lasting existence.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse calls love of God the length of one's days.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Souls that minister the word are rain clouds, and Moses is one.
comments.comment: … Souls ministering to the 'word of salvation' happen to be 'clouds being filled with rain.' Moses, being a single 'cloud,' says: 'let my utterance be expected like rain' (Deut 32:2). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the rain of Moses' teaching as a figure for those who minister the word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A spiritual dew descends from the heavenly light of him who came as light into the world.
comments.comment: Upon these mountains descends a spiritual dew, regarding which Moses said, 'And I will come down as dew' (Deuteronomy 32:2), and in the prophet, 'For the dew from you is its essence' (Isaiah 26:19). From this heavenly dew, the habitation of the blessed shall be from heaven. This spiritual dew does not descend from random clouds, but from the celestial light of the one saying, 'I have come as light into the world' (John 12:46). For this light both dews and shines from above, and makes things to become in most piercing brightness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's name means his proper quality, and one who has called on it can bring his hearers words like fruitful rain and comforting dew.
comments.comment: … God's proper quality — which I take to be called God's 'name' in the Scriptures: … in Deuteronomy, 'Let my utterance wait as rain; let my words come down as dew, as shower upon grass and as snowfall upon herb: for I have called the name of the Lord' (Deuteronomy 32:2); … he who can utter rain that co-works with his hearers for the fruit-bearing of their souls, and bring forth words like dew — comforting words — and by the rush of well-built speeches bring upon his hearers most profitable rain or most useful snowfall — can do these things for this reason. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God is called faithful because he is worthy of being believed and unchangeable in nature, not because he believes.
comments.comment: … It is called faithful not from the act of believing, but from the worthiness of being believed, just as the Word 'Faithful' is said of the Faithful One, and concerning God it is said, 'God is faithful and there is no injustice in him' (Deuteronomy 32:4) and 'God is faithful through whom you were called' (1 Cor 1:9). For because of worthiness and the being worthy of being believed, it was so named, but also because of the certain and unchangeable nature. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense God is called faithful.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture calls God's works true to set them apart from the things of sense, none of which is true.
comments.comment: … And, in a word, to set them apart from the things of sense, none of which is true, it says: “God, true are his works” (Deuteronomy 32:4). It applies the name “works of God” to some things, and the so-called “works of his hands” to lesser ones. At any rate, when it reproaches certain people through Isaiah, it says: “They do not look upon the works of the Lord, and they do not consider the works of his hands” (Isaiah 5:12). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'true are his works' means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One who repays evil for good is more lawless, as Israel was toward God.
comments.comment: … If he who gives evil instead of evil is lawless, how much more the one who gives evil instead of good is more lawless? Such became toward God the Israel of the wilderness, to whom Moses says in Deuteronomy: 'These generations are crooked and perverse, repaying the Lord' (Deut 32:5).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The angels lead us, since God set the nations' boundaries by their number.
comments.comment: … In acting rightly, we treat the angels; for they are our leaders having taken us from the beginning, 'when the Most High divided the nations' (Deut 32:8) and 'he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of his angels' (Deut 32:8). …
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Moses tells of the division of the nations in this song and again, as history, at the tower in Genesis, and the teaching hidden there is long and mystical.
comments.comment:
We say that Moses, the prophet of God among us and his true servant, sets out in the song of Deuteronomy the following about the division of the earth: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; and his people Jacob became the Lord’s portion, Israel the measured lot of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:8–9).

And the same Moses, in the book entitled Genesis, tells of the division of the nations in the form of a history, as follows: … “The Lord came down,” it says, “to see the city and the tower which the sons of men had built. And the Lord said: Behold, they are one race and all have one language; and this they have begun to do, and now nothing that they set out to do will fail them. Come, let us go down and confound their tongue there, so that none of them may understand the speech of his neighbour. And the Lord scattered them from there over the face of all the earth, and they stopped building the city and the tower. For this reason its name was called Confusion, because there the Lord God confounded the language of all the earth, and from there the Lord God scattered them over the face of all the earth” (Genesis 11:5–9). …

The teaching on these matters is long and mystical … It is enough to present in the manner of a history what is told in a hidden way as though it were history, so that those who are able may work out for themselves what bears on the passage.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who did not move from the east and kept the original language alone became the Lord's portion, under a ruler who did not receive them for punishment.
comments.comment: … if anyone can, as under the figure of a history which has something true in itself and yet also points to something secret, let him see also those who kept the original language [when the tongues were confounded at the tower]: because they did not move “from the east,” they remained in the east and in the eastern language. And let him understand that these alone became the Lord’s portion and his people called “Jacob,” and became also “Israel, the measured lot of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:9). And let these alone be governed by a ruler who did not receive those under him for punishment, as the others did.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Moses adorned Israel with God's tender care, as an eagle that carries its young on its back, and David sings of the same overshadowing.
comments.comment: … The divine Moses said something like this when he adorned Israel with the tender care that comes from God: ‘As an eagle would shelter its nest, and yearned over its young, spreading its wings it received them, and took them up on its back’ (Deuteronomy 32:11). David too sings to every holy one who has made his dwelling in the help of the Most High (Psalm 91:1): ‘He will overshadow you upon his back,’ he says (Psalm 91:4). By ‘back’ I take him to mean the parts just below the neck, the region, as it were, of the shoulders, and not the back as a whole. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of the eagle bearing its young.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Deuteronomy calls God the one who begot his people, yet the passage shows the sons blameworthy, and firm sonship is not seen among the ancients.
comments.comment: … That God has been called Father, and that those who have come to the word of God are sons, can be seen in many places — as in Deuteronomy: 'Thou hast forsaken God who begot thee, and forgotten God who nourishes thee' (Deuteronomy 32:6,18,20) … If, then, God is called Father, and those begotten by the word of faith in him are sons, yet the firm and unfallen character of sonship is not to be seen among the ancients. At any rate the very passages we set out show those called sons to be blameworthy …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because of the sins of the Hebrew people, God chose the foolish things of the world and made a senseless nation versed in divine words.
comments.comment: The prophets also foretold this: that because of the sins of the Hebrew people God would choose not one nation but picked people from every quarter, and that, choosing “the foolish things of the world” (1 Corinthians 1:27), he would make the senseless nation (compare Deuteronomy 32:21) become versed in the divine words, with the kingdom of God taken from them and given to these (Matthew 21:43). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the senseless nation is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God guides even those who are not sensible, as he foretold through Moses of the senseless nation and Paul said of the foolish things of the world.
comments.comment:
… God, giving laws in Jesus to men everywhere, guides even those who are not sensible, so far as such people can be guided toward the better.

The God who speaks in Moses knew this, as we have also said above, and says: “They moved me to jealousy with what is no god; they provoked me to anger with their idols; and I will move them to jealousy with what is no nation; with a senseless nation I will provoke them to anger” (Deuteronomy 32:21). Knowing it, Paul too said: “God chose the foolish things of the world to put the wise to shame” (1 Corinthians 1:27). …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who honored ungodliness had to be put outside God's mercy, while those caught in sin through ignorance were pitied and called, which Moses' words also say.
comments.comment:
… it was necessary, truly necessary, that those who had held ungodliness toward God in honor should be put outside his sparing mercy and love; but that those who through ignorance had been caught in the pits of sin and had fallen under the devil's hand should be pitied by the Creator of all, and called to the knowledge of him and to the light of the truth.

This, I think, is found in the words of the all-wise Moses too, where he says: 'They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god; they angered me with their carved images. And I will provoke them to jealousy with what is no nation; with a senseless nation I will anger them' (Deuteronomy 32:21). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God turned to the senseless nation.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One must flee godless doctrines, the wine of Sodom's vine.
comments.comment: As, then, it is salutary to abstain from the flesh of the dragon — and the flesh of the dragon is godless doctrines and false opinions — so it is beneficial and choiceworthy to refuse and flee 'the grape gathered from the vine of Sodom' and the wine gathered from it, being 'the fury of dragons and the incurable fury of asps' (Deuteronomy 32:32-33). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Vengeance is his, so patience is ours and he rewards it.
comments.comment: … He promises this to us, saying: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay (Romans 12:19; Deuteronomy 32:35)—that is, patience is yours, and I will reward patience. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what leaving vengeance to the Lord means.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: By dying to the flesh we gain birth in the Spirit, as the Lord says he kills and makes alive.
comments.comment: … But I am about to speak of spiritual rebirth, and so I place death before life. For by dying to the flesh we gain birth in the Spirit, as the Lord also says: "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). Let us die, then, so that we may live. …
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: God puts to death those who live in wickedness and brings in a better life, as a physician cuts to remove what harms.
comments.comment: … For they too seem to have heard “I will kill,” and they often throw it in our faces, but “I will make alive” (Deuteronomy 32:39) they do not even remember. Yet the whole saying shows that those who live to the common harm and act out of wickedness are put to death by God, and that a better life is brought in for them in its place, the life God would give to those who have died to sin (Romans 6:2). In the same way they have heard “I will strike,” but they do not go on to see “and I will heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39). That is like what a physician might say who has cut into bodies and made severe wounds in order to remove what harms them and stands in the way of health …
comments.selected_reason: Explains that 'I kill' is followed by 'I make alive' and 'I will strike' by 'I will heal'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture names the grim things first and the cheerful ones second, so God kills first and then makes alive, as with Paul.
comments.comment: … And we have always watched in Scripture that the things which look grim, if I may call them so, are named first, then the things that seem cheerful are said second. 'I will kill and I will make alive.' (Deuteronomy 32:39) He did not say, 'I will make alive,' and after that, 'I will kill.' For it is impossible that what God has made alive should be taken away by him or by anyone else. But 'I will kill and I will make alive.' (Deuteronomy 32:39) Whom will I kill? Paul the betrayer, Paul the persecutor. 'And I will make alive,' (Deuteronomy 32:39) so that he may become 'Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ.' (1 Corinthians 1:1)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In many places the sword signifies punishment, as in the Lord's sword devouring blood.
comments.comment: … In many places of the Scriptures the sword signifies punishment, as in: 'I will drink my arrows, and my sword devours the blood of the wounded' (Deuteronomy 32:42), and: 'my sword was drunken in heaven' (Isaiah 34:5); …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The call to rejoice is for all nations at once, not one Hebrew nation.
comments.comment: Concerning the simultaneous joy and delight of all men, it has been written: 'Rejoice, O nations, with his people' (Deuteronomy 32:43), no longer of one single Hebrew nation, but of all at once worshiping and serving God …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is called to rejoice with the Lord's people.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word of God calls only those worthy of God men of God, such as Moses, and will not call anything wicked his possession.
comments.comment: … the word of God is unwilling to call anything wicked God’s possession, since it judges such a thing unworthy of so great a Lord. That is why not all men are called men of God, but only those who are worthy of God, such as Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1) and Elijah (1 Kings 17:24), and anyone else who is recorded as “a man of God,” or who is like those so recorded.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the title 'man of God' given to Moses.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Moses blessed Joseph's tribe with the seasons, dew and sun's turnings, which make the earth fruitful.
comments.comment: … And Moses, blessing the tribe of Joseph, gives blessings from the seasons of heaven and the dew, and from the sun's turnings and the meetings of months, and from the tops of mountains and everlasting hills (Deuteronomy 33:13-15), since the region around the earth is made fruitful through the good order in these things. …
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: The charge the Jew brings against Jesus could be turned on Moses, who wrote that no one knows his burial, so dignifying it.
comments.comment: For just as the Jew makes it a charge that Jesus foretold that after dying he would rise again, so the man who argues the like about Moses will reply to the one who says this that Moses too wrote (for Deuteronomy also is his) that “no one knows his burial to this day” (Deuteronomy 34:6), dignifying and exalting even his burial as unknown to the human race.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
